SUE Design Manager User Guide

Chapter 1

Overview

Introduction

SUE is much more that just another schematic capture tool. It is a complete visual design, simulation, and documentation system. It netlists to multiple formats with the ability to swap behavioral for structural models, drives many simulators directly, displays simulation results either directly onto the schematics or onto waveform viewers, ties documentation to schematics, etc. And then there is the SUE Data Path Compiler (DPC)...

This document is meant to provide an overview of the basic concepts of SUE. It is not meant to explain all of its features, nor does it even try to. Instead, it is assumed that the best way to learn SUE is to understand the basic concepts discussed below and then to experiment with the tool itself.

Example:

If you don't understand how the busing works, draw some simple schematics in SUE that have buses, netlist them, and look at the netlist files. For an even faster example, run generate term names, select some associated wires, and look in the SUE message window to see what SUE has named them.

You should also consult the README file, the .suerc file (described in the section "User Customization"), and the SUE FAQ, and run through the Micro Magic Tools SUE Tutorial.

SUE Philosophy

SUE tries to maintain a very simple, intuitive user interface. Even so, SUE provides many forms of on-line help. Most common commands have hotkeys associated with them which are displayed next to the menu item and also in the hotkey help window which pops up when you hit the Space help key. Advanced users find that they seldom need to use the menus and typically run SUE from hotkeys and mousing, which greatly speeds design.

SUE also attempts to provide a completely deterministic user interface, requiring no guesswork on the user's part. For example, clicking Button-1 will always select the highlighted object, and thus you should never be surprised at what item gets selected. Furthermore, if the highlighted item is not the desired item, simply move the mouse until the desired item becomes highlighted. You should never need to click randomly in order to select the desired item. For this to be true, you must completely understand the next few sections about objects and selection.

Objects in SUE

SUE only permits a short list of objects to be drawn or manipulated. These are: 

      instances of icons 
      wires 
      lines 
      arcs 
      text 
     

While this list appears limited, after a while you will find it is sufficient for most applications.

Note that circles and ovals are a subset of arcs whose extent is large enough to make them appear closed. Furthermore, a rectangle is not a true object in SUE, but rather a line whose segments are configured to be a rectangle. Despite not having rectangle objects as such, SUE does allow the user to create and manipulate rectangles as if they were primitive objects.

In addition, three other object types sometimes appear: 

      open dots 
      solder dots 
      icon origin 
     

These later objects are managed entirely by SUE and are automatically generated and not saved in output files. Dots display connectivity.

Some SUE functions add temporary objects to a schematic or icon. These temporary objects are a different color than any of the four states of regular objects (all colors are specified in the .suerc file), and disappear when any of the selection commands are invoked (for example, by clicking Button-1).

Examples of temporary objects are text anchors, which are visible when adding/editing text or by invoking the menu command show text anchors, and the zoom and selection boxes.

The Four States

Objects can have one of four states, signified by different colors: 

      active, 
      selected, 
      active/selected, or 
      none 
     

An object's state, and hence color, is a temporary attribute and is neither saved, printed, nor does it affect operations like netlisting. Other than to signify an object's state, SUE does not use colors nor permit them for comments or other uses. Note that temporary objects get a separate, unique color.

When the cursor moves over an object, SUE changes the color of that object to signify that it is the active object. We say that this object is highlighted. Only one object can be active at a given time.

Icons are treated as a single object so that if the cursor covers any part of an icon, the whole icon will become active. Therefore, if you are unsure, for example, whether a piece of text is part of the nearby icon, simply move the cursor over the text. If the entire icon is highlighted, then it is part of the icon, otherwise it isn't.


You must move the cursor over a visible part of the icon to highlight it. You cannot simply put the cursor in the center of the object.

Some SUE functions, like selection, operate on the active object, for example:

  • Clicking Button-1 on the active object will select it. Because SUE changes the active object's color, you should never have to guess what object is nearest to the cursor if there is some ambiguity.

  • If you are trying to select a particular object and there are nearby or overlapping objects, you might have to move the cursor around a bit to activate the desired object.

  • If you can't find any position on or nearby the desired object that will activate it, don't despair. You can always select one or more of the nearby objects and move them away to give you a clean shot at the desired object.

  • Alternatively, you can use the menu item lower in the Edit menu to lower the selected item to the bottom of the display list. This has the effect of placing the offending object below the desired object, which should provide you with easy access to the desired object.

Most SUE functions operate on the selected objects as opposed to the active objects (an object that is both active/selected is included in this list). Unlike the active object, more than one object can be selected at a time.

  • To move a section of a schematic you might first select a number of objects and then move them all with the move command or Button-2/3.

Some commands depend on both the selected and active objects, for example:

  • If you click Button-2 over an active/selected object, that object and all other selected objects will be moved. However,

  • If you click Button-2 over an active object (not selected), all other objects will be deselected, the active object will then be selected, and then only that object will be moved (since it is then the only selected object).

Connectivity

In SUE, what you see is what's connected. Connectivity is determined by proximity and denoted with either:

  • a hollow square (open dot) - unconnected

  • nothing - two connections at the point

  • a solid square (solder dot) - more than two connections

Notice the difference between the smaller solid squares that denote terminals on icons, with the larger solid squares that are solder dots.

Open dots and solder dots are not actual objects, but are computed and displayed to show the user what SUE thinks is or is not connected.

  • If SUE draws an open dot where you think there should be a solder dot, click Button-2 over the offending wire and SUE will recompute the associated connectivity. This works the same way for solid dots.

Orientations

Icons can be flipped on both X- and Y-axes and rotated. Each of the eight possible orientations has a short moniker: 

      R0 			not flipped or rotated 
      RX 			flipped in X (around the Y axis) 
      RY 			flipped in Y (around the X axis) 
      RXY 			flipped in both X and Y 
      R90 			rotated 90 degrees clockwise 
      R270 			rotated 270 degrees clockwise 
      R90X 			flipped in X and then rotated 90 degrees clockwise 
      R90Y 			flipped in Y and then rotated 90 degrees clockwise 
     

Selected items can be flipped and rotated with the commands flip sideways, flip upsidedown, and rotate, all of which are in the Edit menu. Note that flipping or rotating an object can break its connectivity, as will be apparent. Placing the icon origin at the center of the icon helps minimize this possibility.

Default Bindings

Emacs is the official editor of SUE. This means that whenever you are presented with a text entry opportunity in SUE, simple Emacs bindings should work, such as:

Ctrl-d for delete next character,

Ctrl-k for kill to end of line,

Ctrl-b for back one character,

Ctrl-n and Ctrl-p for next and previous line,

and so on.

In addition, the arrow keys, Tab, Delete, and Back Space should all do the appropriate things. The Escape key will cancel all menus as should Control-c.

Miscellany

The window in which you started SUE becomes a Tcl interpreter that allows you to directly examine and manipulate the SUE database or issue shell commands such as changing the working directory. This window is also referred to as the command line. Furthermore, SUE will post status, completion and error messages to this window, and thus it is important that this window be visible when using SUE.

If you have two displays (assuming you are typing into display :0.0), it is sometimes useful to start SUE with: 

      sue -display :0.1

so that the command line window is in a different display than the schematics window.



The "-display" switch must be the first switch.

Tcl and also SUE are case sensitive. Since SPICE converts all net names to lower case, the SPICE cross-prober in SUE will do the same.

Variables and properties in SUE often have binary values, either true or false. You cannot use the strings true or false; instead use the following:

      • true <— 1

      • false <— 0 or "" or undefined

On-line Help

SUE displays short messages in the upper right-hand section of the main window, which is called the SUE message window. The message window normally contains information about the selected object. When traversing the menus, the message window instead displays a short description of the menu function beneath the cursor. Finally, during operations which require multiple button clicks or key strokes, the message window displays key strokes needed to complete or abort the operation. If the message gets erased or is too long to fit into the message window, you can always hit the Space help key, which displays the message in its entirety along with all current hotkey bindings.

If a single object is selected, SUE displays the known information about that object in the message window.

Observe that if multiple objects are selected, SUE displays the object with the lowest ID.

For example, the message window might contain: 

      selected: nand2 R0 #10 (Xnand2_1)

where nand2 is the name of the selected icon, R0 is its orientation (that is, not rotated or mirrored) and #10 is the internal ID of the object, which is a unique identifier for this schematic. If the schematic has been netlisted, the unique local instance name used in the netlist will also be displayed in parentheses; here it is Xnand2_1.

If a segment of a wire is selected instead, the message window might contain: 

      selected: wire #139 (net_23)

In this case, only the type (for example, wire), the ID, and the net name (if already netlisted) are shown. This net name is the local net name of the net and will be concatenated with its path to this point in the netlist. Nevertheless, this net name is useful in determining how SUE has named otherwise unnamed wires and determining if buses are appropriately constructed.

For SUE operations which require multiple button clicks or key strokes, the standard button assignments and hot-keys are often replaced or augmented. These complex operations are called modes. SUE has the following modes: 

      wire  
      line 
      arc  
      text  
      icon  
      duplication  
      replace 
      move  
      select region  
      zoom  
      pan

In a SUE mode, the message window will describe the hotkeys and button assignments which are valid in that mode. Hitting the help key Space will also display this message in its entirety and explicitly list all hotkey definitions that are valid. Unfortunately, you cannot zoom in or out in a mode, which might be handy when moving objects or drawing wires, for example. Instead, SUE will auto-pan the screen when you reach a border.


Ctrl-c will always abort a mode, leaving the cell in the state it was in before you entered the mode.

Example:

When adding lines or rectangles, the message window first contains the following line: 

      Button-1 starts line segments, Button-2/3 start rectangle, Ctrl-c aborts.

Once Button-1 (the left mouse button) has been pressed above the desired location on the screen to start the line, the message window changes to the following: 

      Button-1 starts new segment, Button-2/3 ends, Delete removes last segment, Ctrl-c aborts.

which should be self explanatory. If the message gets erased or is too long to fit into the message window, you can always hit the Space help key, which displays the entire message along with all current hotkey bindings.

SUE's cursor changes depending its status. When SUE is waiting for user input and isn't in any mode, the cursor is a pointer. When in a mode, the cursor changes to a finger. If SUE is busy then the cursor becomes the cartoon character gumby to keep you company. Finally, when SUE is waiting for input from a popup menu or window, the cursor becomes a "?" (question mark).

If SUE is not responding to commands, check the cursor. It is possible that SUE is waiting for you to complete a menu. Remember that if you Ctrl-z out of SUE, SUE will not respond until you bring it to the foreground again.

Mousing

Most simple commands in SUE, like selecting and moving objects, are done entirely with the mouse and may not be listed in any menu. Furthermore, these commands are context sensitive, meaning their function depends on what is highlighted. For example, pressing Button-1 when nothing is selected begins a select region command that lets you drag a selection box. However, pressing Button-1 over a highlighted object simply selects that item. Finally, pressing Button-1 over an item in the Schematic List box goes to that schematic, while pressing Button-1 over an item in an Icon List box adds an instance of that icon to the current schematic. This may sound confusing and a little bewildering to the novice user, but with a little practice becomes second nature.

How can you decipher all combinations of button clicks, especially if they aren't listed in the menus? Use the Space help key. You can hit the Space help key at any time and in any place. If you hit the help key in a mode, you will see the unique bindings for that mode. If you hit the help key over the Schematics List box, you will see the bindings for it, etc. Remember to look for the context-sensitive bindings that are displayed in the help key window near the bottom.

As a starting point, listed below are some of the common mouse bindings.

Table 1: Common Mouse-Button Bindings

Function Button Object
select Button-1 any
drag select box Button-1 none
toggle select shift-Button-1 any
select and move Button-2/3 any, not selected
move selected Button-2/3 any if selected or none
add select and move Shift-Button-2/3 any
edit icon properties Double-Button-1 icon
edit generator props Shift-Double-Button-1 generator
highlight wire Double-Button-1 wire
highlight wire to node wire Shift-Double-Button-1 wire
highlight wire by name Control-Double-Button-1 wire
edit text Double-Button-1 text
edit line Double-Button-1 line
edit arc Double-Button-1 arc
edit schematic Button-1 Schematic menu
edit schematic's icon Shift-Button-1 Schematic menu
add icon to schematic Button-1 Icon menu
edit schematic Shift-Button-1 Icon menu
edit icon Button-2 Icon menu

Buttons 2 and 3, as much as possible, execute the same command. This allows SUE to work nearly as well for two- as well as three-button mice.

User Customization

All of the user-customizable options in SUE, including pointers to tools, hotkey definitions, colors, and more, are located in .suerc files (for SUE Run Commands). These files are sourced from Tcl and thus require correct Tcl syntax. SUE sources more than one .suerc file to allow for site-specific, user-specific, and project-specific customization. Since the .suerc files are sourced from Tcl, you can also define Tcl procedures in them and source your own Tcl files from them.

At startup, SUE first sources the file ${MMI_TOOLS}/sue/.suerc (or the system .suerc). This .suerc file comes with every new release of the software and you should not modify it. When you get a new version of the software, it will probably include new options that are included in this .suerc file.

Next, SUE attempts to source the file ${MMI_TOOLS}/../mmi_local/sue/.suerc (or the site .suerc), if it exists, which will overwrite any defaults in the system .suerc. The site .suerc should be set up to include all site-dependent options such as the commands for running tools and automatic inclusion of common libraries.

Next, SUE attempts to source ~/.suerc (from the user's home directory, the user .suerc) and then ~/mmi_private/sue/.suerc (the user's private .suerc). The private .suerc is included so users don't have to clutter up their home directories with various Micro Magic Tools files. Finally, SUE will attempt to source ./.suerc (for example, from the current directory, the local .suerc) if it exists. Definitions in the most recently loaded .suerc file will replace any previous definitions. These latter three .suerc files allow users to customize their personal SUE environments.

You should look through the system .suerc file to understand what customizations are possible. Only a small subset of the possible customizations are described in this manual. To change a particular feature, however, only copy that feature into the site, user, private, or local .suerc file and then modify it. Do not copy the entire .suerc file into your site/user/private/local version, since then you won't automatically realize changes in the system .suerc file from new releases or changes that the SUE administrator might make in the site .suerc, such as redefining a tool location.

You should place your personal customizations, such as SUE colors and window geometry defaults, in the user ~/.suerc or private ~/mmi_private/sue/.suerc file. Only place project customizations in the user/private file or possibly the site .suerc or you will be constantly duplicating this file. Good customizations here are specifying what libraries to load and autoload. For example, to autoload all of the icons in the ./icon_lib directory, add the following line to your ./.suerc file: 

      lappend AUTOLIB ./icon_lib


It is strongly advised that you don't modify the hotkeys or, if you must, you only modify one or two. If individuals change the hotkeys indiscriminately, soon, no one will be able help anyone else on their workstation because of incompatibilities.

If you want to run SUE without loading all of the .suerc files described, you can override the loading of any file with the UNIX environment variable SUE_IGNORE_SUERC. This feature is useful for debugging .suerc files or ignoring specific customizations. To ignore all .suerc files, use the line: 

      setenv SUE_IGNORE_SUERC site,user,private,local

You can use any subset of this line to ignore only specific .suerc files. For example to only ignore the user .suerc file, set: 

      setenv SUE_IGNORE_SUERC user

Schematics and Icons

SUE understands two types of drawings: schematics and icons, which are sometimes called symbols in other tools.

Schematics can contain instances of icons, wires, lines, arcs, and text (in other words, everything).

In contrast, icons are primarily pictures. Icons placed into schematics are immutable objects that cannot be broken apart or changed. To change or create an icon, you must edit the cell's icon view, in which all of the pieces of the icon, the lines, arcs, text, terminals, etc., are separate and mutable. Basically everything that you see in the icon view will be displayed when you instantiate the icon, with the following exceptions:

    • terminals (representing inputs, outputs, and inouts) are a special type of icon which are displayed as small squares when the icon is instantiated.

    • properties (that is, text beginning with a "-") which are not displayed. See "Chapter 1, Parameterized Icons" on page XX.

    • title bars which are only displayed in the icon view and are for documentation purposes only.

All other icons placed into an icon will magically disappear when you leave the icon because they don't belong there.

Example:

If you wanted to make an icon of a "nand" gate and you already had a respectable icon of an "and" gate, you wouldn't put the "and" gate icon into the "nand" gate's icon view. Instead you would go to the "and" gate's icon view and copy to clipboard the lines and arcs that make up the "and" gate. You would then go to the "nand" gate's icon view and paste those items there.

In general, cells have both a schematic and an icon. Both the schematic and icon are automatically associated together by having the same name.

Furthermore, schematic/icon pairs are automatically saved together in the same file. Some schematics, such as top level schematics, have no icons. In addition, some icons have no schematics, for example, primitives such as fets and capacitors.

You cannot simply rename cells in SUE. Instead, you must copy the cell to a new name and then save it out (if desired). Any reference to the original cell name must also be changed. For example, let's say you have a schematic named "foo" and inside of it you have instantiated an instance of "qux". Now let's say you want to rename "qux" to "bar". You go to "qux" and hit copy in the File menu and enter the new name. If you now go back to "foo", you will see that "qux" is still there. Now you have to replace "qux" with "bar". Moral: name your cells carefully.

All terminals of associated schematic/icon pairs should match for correct netlisting. If they don't match, the netlister doesn't know which schematic terminals correspond to which icon terminals and will display an error telling you where the mismatch is. Otherwise, SUE is mostly oblivious to terminals.

When creating a new icon for a schematic, SUE will automatically generate input, output, and inout terminals in the icon to match the schematic. A magical mechanism will also try to rename and add terminals into the other view to match whatever damage you are doing. However, this mechanism is not perfect and doesn't even try to delete terminals in the other view. One simple way to break it is by trying to swap the names of two terminals.

Icons need a reference point for placement into schematics and for orientation. This reference point is called the icon origin (represented by a "+" in the drawing) and is required in all icons. In contrast, schematics require no reference point and thus have no displayed origin. The icon origin can be moved but not duplicated or deleted. Thus, to move an icon relative to its origin, you can selected the icon components and move them or you can just select the icon origin and move it. The origin of the icon is displayed as a point when the icon is instantiated in a schematic. All rotations/mirroring will occur about that point.

      • If you move the origin in the icon, any instantiated icons of that name in schematics will move in the schematics since their position relative to their origin has moved. If you are not careful this will reposition any existing schematics that have this icon in them, probably disconnecting its terminals from the schematic's wires.

      • If you substitute one icon for a different type using the command replace instance in the Edit menu, the origin of the new icon will be placed where the origin of the old icon was. Therefore, try to maintain consistent origin placement in icons.

Terminals placed in icons will appear as small solid squares when that icon is instantiated. These terminals, along with wires, will display connection information as described above.

      • For icon terminal names to be visible when the icon is instantiated, add a text object in the icon for each terminal.

      • If the name of the terminal is changed, the user is required to changed this text object if the different name is desired in the instantiated icon. This is not automatic.


The duplicate text feature is very handy for placing text next to I/O's in icons.

By using the show sel. term names function in the View menu, you can display the true names of the terminals in the selected icon in a schematic.

All icons that SUE knows about can be found in the Icon Library List boxes. Icons that are in the autoload path but not yet loaded will not appear in the list box.

  • To instantiate one of these icons into an existing schematic, just click on the icon name in the List box and that icon can then be dropped into the schematic.

  • Another way to create an icon is to just duplicate an existing icon in a schematic.

  • Double-clicking an instantiated icon will bring up an Edit Properties popup that allows you to edit the properties of that individual icon such as, for example, the width (W) and length (L) of an nfet.

  • Click Button-2 (the middle mouse button) on an icon in the Icon List box, and SUE will display the icon for editing.

See the "Mousing" section for a list of button actions, or hit the Space help key in SUE.

Icon Library List Boxes

There are three forms of Icon Library List boxes: Flat, Hier, and Include. The type of list box used by SUE is determined by the .suerc file. Note that Include is the default form and the other two may be removed in future versions of SUE.

When the Flat Icons List box is selected, all icons that SUE knows about are displayed alphabetically in one list box. This approach is convenient when dealing with relatively small circuits or with few icons.

When the Hier Icons List box is selected, multiple icons list boxes are displayed and each list box only displays the icons that were loaded from a single directory. This directory is shown in the first line of the list box.

  • If you click on the directory name, a menu gives you the option of adding another list box, deleting the current one, or changing which directory of icons are displayed in this list box.

  • Use the command raise windows under the File menu to help you get them back.

In addition, SUE attempts to iconify and deiconify all windows together.

The third and default form of list box is called Include. Include is identical to Hier except that all the List boxes are included in the main window instead of being separate top level windows. This is especially handy if you tend to "lose" list boxes because they get covered by other windows.

All of the commands described above for dropping icons into schematics and otherwise manipulating icons are identical between the Flat, Hier, and Include list boxes.

If you want to see all of the icons from a given directory in the Icons List box, you can click on Autoload directory in the menu at the top of the desired icons' list box. You can get this same functionality at startup by adding the directory to the AUTOLIB global variable in the .suerc file, for example: 

      lappend AUTOLIB <dir_name>

or starting SUE with the "-AUTOLIB" switch, for example: 

      sue -AUTOLIB <dir_name>

In contrast, only schematics that have been pushed into (or previously viewed) are shown in the Schematics List box. SUE only loads cells on demand, so a circuit with a large hierarchy will still come up quickly since SUE ignores the hierarchy until it is required to do something with it, like display it or netlist it.

  • For example, if you load the schematic "a" which contains instances of icons for schematics "b" and "c", initially only the schematic "a" will appear in the Schematics List box.

  • Only when you push into "b" and see its schematic will "b" appear in the Schematics List box, and similarly for "c".


    During netlisting, the netlister will first push into every schematic that it requires, which may not be all or even any of them because of disk caching.

Changing the displayed schematic is as easy as clicking on the desired schematic in the Schematics List box. However, if you have a hierarchy of cells, it is best to get to cells by pushing into icons and popping out of schematics. This is especially important when cross-probing, since the hierarchical path is required to get the net name correct. Whenever you change schematics using the Schematics List box, SUE has no way of knowing the hierarchy of the current cell and thus resets it. Thus, you can never pop out of a schematic that you went to using the Schematics List box.

  • When netlisting, the hierarchy is reset so that the current schematic is the root. Before netlisting, you must pop up to the desired root schematic or go directly to that schematic via the Schematics List box.

The title frame of the main window (or the top banner on the X window) of SUE will display certain pertinent information about the schematic or icon in that window such as its name, type (either S or I for Schematic or Icon), modification flag, written flag, full pathname, and netlisting mode in parentheses. For example, if you are currently editing the schematic "foo" and you have modified it but haven't saved it yet, your title frame will show: 

      SUE: foo SM  /home/luser/circuits/foo.sue (verilog) 
      
     

The current netlist type, Verilog in this case, is displayed in the title frame along with the first two items in the Sim menu. Furthermore, the modified flag will be displayed in front of the appropriate schematic or icon names in the Schematics List and Icons List boxes. It is a good idea to look at the full pathname of the current cell periodically to insure that you are indeed working with the desired cell.

SUE Files and Libraries

SUE files are human readable and normally have the suffix of .sue as determined by the .suerc file. The actual SUE file format is described below. When saving a file over an existing file, the old one is first moved to .BAK before the new one is saved out.

SUE attempts to write files back to the same directory that it reads them from, even if you change the current working directory. You can always know where SUE will write a particular cell, since its full pathname is listed in the title frame of the X window.

  • If you want to write the file to a different directory, first use the Change Path command in the File menu to change its directory and then save it.

Whenever you save a schematic in SUE, only that schematic and its associated icon (if one exists) are written to a file with the name of .sue. Similarly, if you are displaying an icon, then the associated schematic (if one exists) will also be saved. Icons and schematics are automatically associated if they have the same name.



Icons of schematics instantiated in the current schematic are NOT saved.

When you read in a schematic, all of the instantiated icons must be available to SUE. These cells must be in files in the same directory as the schematic or in libraries (or directories) known to SUE.

SUE uses the automatic loading feature of Tcl to manage libraries. In short, directories in the automatic loading path are kept in the Tcl variable auto_path, which is automatically managed by SUE. In each directory, the file tclIndex must be maintained (also automatically managed by SUE) which associates Tcl procedures with the files in that directory that contain them.

Since SUE schematics and icons are saved as Tcl procedures, a library then consists of simply a directory of .sue files. In order for SUE to recognize this library, the directory name need only be added to the auto_path variable. When loading a .sue file, SUE will automatically add the directory of that file to the auto_path if it isn't already there and regenerate the appropriate tclIndex if needed. Thus, all of the .sue files in that directory will then be automatically available as icons in the loaded schematic. Otherwise, libraries can be included when bringing up SUE with the -LIB or -AUTOLIB options or adding options to the .suerc file (see the README).


SUE attempts to regenerate the tclIndex file when required using a variant of the Tcl command auto_mkindex. However, the tclIndex file can become stale if you UNIX move files into or out of directories during a SUE session.

For more information about auto loading see the Tcl manual or online Tcl man pages.

Because of the automatic loading feature, schematics and icons in libraries will only be loaded when they are specifically asked for. Thus even if your library is in the auto_path it will not be visible to you unless you AUTOLIB it. Alternatively, you can view all of the cells in the library by clicking on Autoload directory in the menu at the top of the desired Icon List boxes.

  • For example, if you want to instantiate the mux2 icon that's in your library into your current schematic, you will first have to explicitly load mux2.sue from the library directory. It will then appear in the Icons List box (and possibly in the Schematics List box if it also has a schematic). Now you can place it into your schematic. The good news is that the next time you enter SUE and bring up the same schematic, it will automatically bring in the mux2 cell (assuming your auto_path is still correct).

If you have two cells with the same name that are both in your auto_path, SUE might load the wrong one. SUE cannot handle two different cells with the same name and different paths. Since SUE automatically manages the auto_path, it is difficult to insure that the auto_path order will be correct.

If you have a schematic called foo in foo.sue and you UNIX copy (cp) that file to bogus.sue, the procedure SCHEMATIC_foo in bogus.sue can shadow the schematic SCHEMATIC_foo in foo.sue which is the one you really want.

A common error is to UNIX copy a file, for example, from foo.sue to foo_save.sue. Don't do this. If you want to make a special backup of the file, call it something like foo.sue.save. Since this latter file name doesn't have the suffix .sue, SUE will ignore it when autoloading.

  • To prevent this problem, always UNIX copy files to filenames with suffixes other than .sue or .tcl. Thus, in the previous example, you should copy foo.sue to foo.sue.bogus.

To sum up, demons lurk here so BEWARE!

  • If you suspect that something might be loading incorrectly, or simply want to insure that your SUE file system is consistent, run the check file system command in the File menu. This procedure will report any discrepancies in the SUE file system to the SUE command window.

Unfortunately, you cannot rename schematics or icons by merely renaming their .sue files in UNIX. However, you can UNIX mv or cp (move or copy) them to other directories without any problems as long as you keep the file name the same.

  • You should copy the schematic or icon in SUE using the copy command in the File menu to a new file name and then save it out.

  • If you are intent on using Emacs (or vi) to generate new schematics/icons, then you will probably quickly see that if you want to rename foo.sue to be bar.sue then you will have to change the procedure names SCHEMATIC_foo and ICON_foo in foo.sue to be SCHEMATIC_bar and ICON_bar.

See, that's not so hard.

Default Libraries

Whenever you run SUE, you always want some default libraries. Of these, the devices Library is the most important. The devices Library contains I/O's, globals, name_nets, title bars, and other important special-purpose icons for use in SUE. Typically, you won't ever need to modify these icons. However, you might want to move them or add icons to them. The pathname of this library is kept in the variable SCHEM_DIR(devices) and is set, by default, to be: 

      set SCHEM_DIR(devices) $SUE_DIR/schematics/devices 
     

Typically, you need at least one more set of icons to do anything in SUE. If you are working with SPICE, this set is probably one of the spice or mspice Libraries. If you are working in Verilog, this might be a standard cell library. The library pathname stored in the variable SCHEM_DIR($NETLIST_TYPE) will also be autoloaded at startup.


All libraries other than the devices library are provided simply as examples. If you do not like the way they work, change them. They are not intrinsically a part of SUE.

Wires vs. Lines

Wires are used for making electrical connection. Lines are used for drawing nice pictures. Current doesn't flow in lines - don't try to make it.

You can tell when you have accidentally used a line when you meant to use a wire because no connection information will appear (no solder dots or opens). The message window will also alert you as to the type of object which is selected if there is a doubt. Also, notice that lines can be multi-segment, but that all wires are single-segment; in other words, if you place the mouse over what you think is a wire and more than one segment highlights, then it is a line.

Using wires for drawing is less problematic but should still be avoided. Since icons are merely pictorial, wires have no place in them. Consequently, SUE will automatically convert all wires drawn in icons into lines when saving out icons. SUE will also try to prevent you from drawing wires at all in icons.

  • Non-Manhattan wires can be generated by pressing the Shift key when drawing the wire.

SUE does not restrict the drawing or editing of lines to be Manhattan (in other words, do not try the Shift key, it doesn't help). Once you have finished drawing a line, special nodes on the vertices of the line will appear. These nodes are called edit markers, and allow you to edit the line.

Don't like this set of bullet points... Not enough differentiation betw. B-1 and Sh-B-1...... == KM ==

    • If a line does not show its edit marker, you can display the edit markers by double-clicking on the line.

    • Using Button-1 you can move edit markers (and their associated vertices) around.

    • Using Shift-Button-1 you can move edit markers, preserving Manhattan geometries. This is especially useful for editing rectangles.

Furthermore, you can add vertices to and delete vertices from lines using Button-3:

  • If you click Button-3 over an line edit marker, a new vertex and its edit marker will be created offset slightly from the current vertex.

  • If you hold down the Shift key and hit Button-3 (Shift-Button-3), the highlighted line edit marker and its vertex will be deleted.

Text

All text in a SUE icon or schematic is either part of an icon or not. If it is part of an icon, then the entire icon will be highlighted when the cursor is placed over the text, and the text will move and rotate along with that icon. Text in icons cannot be moved or changed with respect to the icon except by editing the icon itself. Of course the contents of the text will often change when you change that icon's properties; for example, if you double-click on an instance of the nand2 icon and change its name to foo, you will see "foo" on the icon.

The only command that directly separates text from an icon is duplicate text in the Edit menu. This command is very useful in labeling icons:

  • Select some or all of the I/O's in an icon and then execute duplicate text. Try it.

Text not in icons can be edited, resized, and rotated independently and in place; that is, not in a popup window but directly on the cell. Text in SUE has the following properties associated with it:

  • rotation

  • size

  • anchor

Text is either normal or rotated clockwise, in which case the text reads from top to bottom.

  • Hit rotate in the Edit menu to rotate selected text.

Text can only be displayed in one rotation and with no flipping; however, the text anchors will rotate or flip as if other orientations exist.

Text is presently limited to three sizes: small, standard (the default), and large. The relative sizes of the small and large fonts can be manipulated in the .suerc file.

      • The text size can be changed using Shift-Button-1,2,3 (small, medium, large) when editing text (once you have double-clicked on it).

In addition to the text size, the text anchor can be changed from west (w), to east (e), to center (c) in icons. This is handy for making icons of the form:

    Figure 1: Demonstration of Text Anchor 
     

In the above case, you would want the text on the left (in1 and in2) to be anchored on the west side (the default) and the text on the right (out1 and out2) to be anchored on the east side. The icon name FOO probably wants its text anchor to be center. These anchors are displayed in the figure above, with the "^" character.

  • When editing text, an anchor mark is displayed and can be moved using Ctrl-Button-1,2,3 for w(est), e(ast), c(enter).

  • Also, you can display anchors for all the text in the cell with the command Show Text Anchors.

Selection

Most functions operate on selected objects.

  • An active object can be selected by clicking Button-1, which will also deselect all other objects.

  • Otherwise, Shift-Button-1 will toggle the active object between selected and unselected without deselecting any other objects.

  • A region of objects can be selected by dragging a selection box over the region.

  • Selection boxes are generated by clicking Button-1 and holding it while dragging out a selection region.

To clearly distinguish between clicking Button-1 to select a single object and to select a region, SUE always selects the active object if there is one. If no object is active, SUE assumes you are dragging a selection region.

  • By hitting the Tab key when dragging a selection region, you can toggle the selection box mode.

By default, the box is stretched with the mouse motion but the alternative mode moves the entire box.

  • Try hitting the Tab key (do not hold it down) while dragging the region select box. The entire box should move without resizing.

  • Hit the Tab key again and now the box should again resize with the new origin.

  • In addition, it is possible to add to the selection by holding down the Shift key while selecting either individual objects or regions.

Double Clicking

On Icons

As described earlier, double-clicking on icons brings up an Edit Properties popup.

On Wires

Double-clicking (Double-Button-1) on wires selects the entire net (though not nets that are connected via net names -- see below).

Shift-Double-Button-1 selects the net up to a node. This is useful for, say, deleting offshoots of a net.

Ctrl-Double-Button-1 will highlight the entire net, including pieces that are connected by name only. Thus if you Ctrl-Double-Button-1 (can you say that three times fast?) on the ground net, for example, you will select all sections of the ground net, even if they aren't connected together in SUE with wires. Remember to netlist or generate terminal names before using this command.

Moving

Moving objects is common enough that Buttons-2/3 have been dedicated to moving. The move command is also available in the Edit menu.

  • When using Button-2/3 to move objects, first a selection is done on the current object just as with Button-1.

(If the current object is already selected, then the selection remains the same.)

  • Holding down the Shift key during movement will constrain movement to either horizontal or vertical only, depending on which direction the movement would be greatest.

Cutting/Pasting

It is often desirable to copy a section of one schematic or icon into another.

  • This can be done by first selecting the desired section, and then clicking on the Copy to Clipboard function in the Edit menu.

  • Next, go to the desired schematic or icon and click the Paste function in the Edit menu, and it's that simple. Note that you now need to move the pasted items to their final resting places just as if you had just used the duplicate command.

  • In addition to the hotkeys, the Copy and Paste keys on most keyboards are bound to these functions.

The SUE clipboard is separate from the standard UNIX clipboard because it must be able to accept SUE graphical objects. The clipboard contents are saved in the file pointed at by the variable CLIPBOARD_FILE in the .suerc file (the default is ~/.clipboard.sue). Thus, items may be pasted into different SUE sessions than from where they originated. Beware that other SUE sessions must have access to the same icon libraries for this to work correctly. Finally, note that this clipboard is only one deep.

Text in popup windows such as Edit Properties can be cut from and pasted to using the standard UNIX cut and paste mechanism. At present, you cannot cut and paste into text objects in schematics or icons.

Undo

SUE implements near infinite undo capability (the default undo stack is set to 100 by the variable UNDO_LEVEL, but can be changed in the .suerc). Each separate schematic and icon have their own independent undo stacks.


SUE only undoes local changes to schematics or icons. It does not undo zooming or selections that do not create changes. It does not undo global changes like changes to generators or underlying icons. Finally, even if you undo a schematic to the point where it was last saved, undo will not remove the modified flag.

At present, redo has not been implemented.
